workspace.title: Circuit Workspace: MNA Solver and Analysis Methods
workspace.intro: The circuit studio is a single interactive schematic canvas. You place sources, passive parts, semiconductors and instruments, wire them together, and a server-side modified nodal analysis engine solves the network while the canvas animates currents and voltages.
workspace.purpose: This workspace models lumped electrical networks in the steady state (DC and phasor AC) and in the time domain (transients, oscilloscope traces). Every wire junction becomes a node, every part becomes a stamp in one linear system, and the analysis panel can replay the same answer as a human-readable derivation by nodal, mesh, superposition, source transformation or Thévenin methods.

model.heading: Kirchhoff's laws as the foundation
model.body: Kirchhoff's current law states that the algebraic sum of currents leaving any node is zero, $\sum I = 0$, because charge cannot accumulate at a lumped node. Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the sum of branch voltages around any closed loop is zero, $\sum V = 0$, because the electric field of a lumped circuit is conservative. Together with each element's constitutive relation, such as $v = iR$ for a resistor, they give exactly as many independent equations as unknowns.

model.heading: Modified nodal analysis
model.body: The solver assembles the block system $\mathbf A\mathbf x = \mathbf z$ with $\mathbf A = \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf G&\mathbf B\\\mathbf C&\mathbf D\end{bmatrix}$. The matrix $\mathbf G$ holds conductance stamps: a diagonal entry $G_{ii}$ sums the conductances touching node $i$, and an off-diagonal entry $G_{ij}$ is the negative of the conductance joining nodes $i$ and $j$. The blocks $\mathbf B$ and $\mathbf C$ couple ideal voltage sources and other branch-current unknowns $\mathbf j$ to the node voltages $\mathbf v$, while $\mathbf i$ collects injected source currents and $\mathbf e$ the source voltages. The ground part fixes the reference node so the matrix is non-singular; a floating sub-circuit or an open loop of current sources makes $\mathbf A$ singular and is reported instead of solved.

model.heading: Phasors and complex impedance
model.body: For sinusoidal sources at angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$ the same stamps are used with complex values. A resistor stays $R$, an inductor contributes $j\omega L$ and a capacitor $\frac{1}{j\omega C}$, so a series branch has $\mathbf Z = R + j\left(\omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}\right)$. The phasor current is $\hat I = \hat V / \mathbf Z$ and the admittance $\mathbf Y = 1/\mathbf Z = G + jB$ is what enters $\mathbf G$. Resonance occurs where the reactive term vanishes, $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$, and the impedance magnitude is then minimal and equal to $R$.

model.heading: Thévenin equivalents and maximum power
model.body: Seen from a chosen pair of terminals, any linear network reduces to a source $V_{th}$ in series with $R_{th}$. The voltage $V_{th}$ is the open-circuit terminal voltage and $R_{th}$ is $V_{oc}/I_{sc}$, or the resistance seen after all independent sources are zeroed. A load receives the maximum power $P = V_{th}^2/(4R_{th})$ only when its resistance equals $R_{th}$, at which point the efficiency is just one half.

model.heading: Transients and time stepping
model.body: A first-order network moves exponentially from its initial value $v_0$ to its final value $V_\infty$ with time constant $\tau = RC$ for capacitors or $\tau = L/R$ for inductors. After $t = 5\tau$ the response is within about $0.7\%$ of the final value. In the time domain each reactive part is replaced by a companion model: backward Euler turns a capacitor into a conductance $g_C = C/\Delta t$ in parallel with a history current source, so the same linear solve advances the circuit one step at a time.

equations: Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws: the node-sum and loop-sum constraints that every solved circuit satisfies.

mapping.term: Sources: DC voltage, DC rail, AC voltage, DC and AC current, 3-phase
mapping.body: A DC voltage source adds a row to $\mathbf B$, $\mathbf C$ and a value to $\mathbf e$, with an adjustable internal resistance. AC sources take magnitude, phase, offset and a frequency between $0.001\text{ Hz}$ and $1\text{ MHz}$ plus a sine, square, sawtooth or triangle waveform; magnitude and phase become the complex entry of $\mathbf e$. Current sources write directly into $\mathbf i$.

The resistance field (from $0.001\text{ }\Omega$ up to $10^{9}\text{ }\Omega$) sets the stamp $1/R$ in $\mathbf G$. Tolerance and power rating do not change the nominal solve but flag overdissipation. Capacitance and inductance set $\tau$ and the companion conductances.
Placing a ground fixes one node voltage to $0$ and removes its row from the system. Without it the matrix has a free common-mode level and the solve cannot be completed.

mapping.term: Run, pause, reset and time readout
mapping.body: The toolbar advances the transient clock $t$ in steps of $\Delta t$ and displays the elapsed time. Reset restores every reactive state to $v_0$ and $i_0$, which sets the initial condition of the exponentials.
The slider scales wall-clock time into simulated time between $0.1\times$ and $4\times$ in steps of $0.05$. It changes how fast the animation plays, not the physics: $\tau$ is unchanged.

mapping.term: Analysis panel: nodal, mesh, superposition, transform, Thévenin
mapping.body: Each method re-derives the solution that $\mathbf A\mathbf x = \mathbf z$ gives. Nodal lists node-voltage KCL equations, mesh colours loops and applies KVL, superposition solves once per independent source, and Thévenin reduces the network seen by a target load picked with the load selector to $V_{th}$ and $R_{th}$.
The oscilloscope samples node voltages versus time from the transient solver, so a charging capacitor appears as the curve $v_C(t)$. The multimeter reads the solved DC or RMS value at its probes.

example.title: Thévenin equivalent and RC charging
example.problem: A $12\text{ V}$ DC source drives $R_1 = 4\text{ k}\Omega$ in series, followed by $R_2 = 12\text{ k}\Omega$ to ground. A capacitor $C = 10\text{ }\mu\text{F}$, initially discharged, is connected across $R_2$. Find the Thévenin equivalent seen by the capacitor, the time constant, and the capacitor voltage at $t = 60\text{ ms}$.

steps.text: Remove the capacitor and compute the open-circuit voltage with the voltage divider.
Zero the source (a short circuit) so $R_1$ and $R_2$ appear in parallel.
The time constant follows from the Thévenin resistance and the capacitance.
With $v_0 = 0$ and $V_\infty = 9\text{ V}$ evaluate the charging law at $t = 60\text{ ms} = 2\tau$, using $e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$.
The initial charging current is $V_{th}/R_{th}$, which the oscilloscope shows as the steepest slope.

example.result: The equivalent is $V_{th} = 9\text{ V}$ with $R_{th} = 3\text{ k}\Omega$, giving $\tau = 30\text{ ms}$ and $v_C \approx 7.78\text{ V}$ after $60\text{ ms}$, about $86\%$ of the final value.

applications.body: Steady-state phasor analysis with $\mathbf Z$ sizes feeders, checks voltage drop and evaluates power factor correction on three-phase supplies.
Thévenin models of divider-based sensors predict loading error on analog inputs, and $\tau = RC$ sets the cut-off of anti-alias filters.
The rise of coil current with $\tau = L/R$ determines actuation time of contactors, valves and brushed motors.
MNA-based simulation verifies bias networks, pull-up values and decoupling transients before a board is fabricated.
Maximum power transfer and source impedance analysis guide battery, regulator and load matching on constrained supplies.
